clue.text: Continue to play with a pseudonymous Bronte

explanation.surface: Someone keeps performing alongside one of the Bronte sisters writing under a pen name.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep performing a part is to carry on acting; Anne Bronte published as Acton Bell.

clue.text: A self-confessed snapper-up of unconsidered trifles

definitions.text: A self-confessed snapper-up of unconsidered trifles

parts.words: A self-confessed snapper-up of unconsidered trifles
parts.note: the pedlar and pickpocket in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale describes himself with exactly these words

explanation.surface: A petty thief owns up to picking up bits and pieces nobody notices.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Winter's Tale the rogue pedlar calls himself a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles.

clue.text: Papa's were across the river ()

parts.note: Papa is Ernest Hemingway, whose novel is titled Across the River and Into the ... with this word to finish it

explanation.surface: Someone's father owned things on the far bank of the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemingway, nicknamed Papa, wrote the novel Across the River and Into the Trees, so his were across the river.

clue.text: Forester's dream is to be after dark horse

parts.note: after dark means at night
a mare is a female horse

explanation.surface: A woodsman longs to go chasing a dark-coloured horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forester' is C. S. Forester, whose story collection The Nightmare gives the definition; the surface reads it as a woodsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad dream is a nightmare, and C. S. Forester used the word as a book title.

clue.text: MacNeice's extreme days

parts.note: Louis MacNeice titled a 1961 poetry collection after the longest and shortest days of the year

explanation.surface: The poet Louis MacNeice lived through some very hard days.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest and shortest days of the year fall at midsummer and midwinter, and MacNeice's 1961 collection bears that title.

clue.text: Yet Jone she goes / Like one of those / Whom purity had

definitions.text: Yet Jone she goes / Like one of those / Whom purity had

parts.words: Yet Jone she goes / Like one of those / Whom purity had
parts.note: a line of verse with its last word missing; the solver supplies the word that completes the rhyme and the sense

explanation.surface: A rustic verse about a girl named Jone who walks along like someone made holy by her innocence.
explanation.definitionFit: Made holy or canonised: those whom purity has blessed are hallowed, and the word rhymes with the verse's pattern.

clue.text: Bishop Arthur Redgauntlet

explanation.surface: A churchman is named alongside a character from a Walter Scott novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Latimer was a Protestant bishop burned in 1555; in Scott's Redgauntlet, Darsie Latimer turns out to be Sir Arthur Darsie Redgauntlet.

clue.text: Dexter's Paris Quintet

explanation.surface: A novelist named Dexter wrote about five people in the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Pete Dexter's novel Paris Trout names its title character; Schubert's piano quintet in A is known as the Trout.

clue.text: French dramatist takes encore ill, collapsing

indicators.note: a collapsing structure falls apart, so the letters of these two words fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A French playwright is called back for an encore while feeling unwell and keels over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapsing' rearranges ENCORE ILL; 'takes' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Corneille was a seventeenth-century French tragic playwright, author of Le Cid.

clue.text: Current hotel in ship for Swedish poet

indicators.note: in tells us that the current and hotel letters sit inside the ship's letters

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
AC is alternating current
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Electricity reaches a hotel on board a liner, all for a poet from Sweden.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelly Sachs, German-born and naturalised in Sweden, shared the 1966 Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: Meredith's unduly subjective subject?

parts.note: George Meredith wrote an 1879 novel whose title character, Sir Willoughby Patterne, is wholly self-absorbed

explanation.surface: A question about what topic Meredith wrote on that was far too personal.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's 1879 novel is named for its self-centred hero, a person who sees everything only through himself.

clue.text: One among Horatio's rich friends

indicators.note: among says the letters needed lie inside the words that follow it

explanation.surface: Someone belongs to the wealthy circle of friends around Hamlet's companion Horatio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' points into horatiOS RICh; the whole clue also describes Hamlet's foppish courtier.
explanation.definitionFit: Osric is the affected, wealthy courtier in Hamlet, part of the court circle that Horatio moves in.

clue.text: One with a leaning, say, for piano works ()

indicators.note: say tells us the word is to be spoken, giving a sound rather than a spelling

parts.note: a ship with a list leans to one side, so a list is a leaning

explanation.surface: Someone with a preference picks out some piano pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The composer's name stands for his piano music, as one might say 'playing Chopin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt's name is used for his body of piano music, the way a composer's name stands for his works.

clue.text: "Let old yield the prize / Or both divide the crown" (Dryden)

definitions.text: "Let old yield the prize / Or both divide the crown" (Dryden)

parts.words: "Let old yield the prize / Or both divide the crown" (Dryden)
parts.note: lines from Dryden's Alexander's Feast with a name missing after 'old'; the solver supplies the musician named there

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dryden urging an old champion to give up the prize or share the honour.
explanation.definitionFit: In Alexander's Feast, Dryden names the Greek musician Timotheus as the one who should yield to Saint Cecilia.

clue.text: Shakepearean clown finds way on Spanish seaside

indicators.note: on places the way after the seaside piece, as in a down light written beneath it

parts.note: costa is Spanish for coast, as in Costa Brava
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: A clown from Shakespeare discovers a path along the Spanish coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Costard is the comic rustic in Love's Labour's Lost.

clue.text: Gardener-poet, sonnets he produced

indicators.note: produced as in brought out or staged, so these letters are reworked into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A poet who was also a gardener wrote sonnets.
explanation.definitionFit: William Shenstone, eighteenth-century poet, made his estate The Leasowes a celebrated landscape garden.

clue.text: River thriller writer mentioned in eighteenth-century periodical

parts.note: Eric Ambler wrote spy thrillers

explanation.surface: A thriller writer from the river gets a mention in an old magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Johnson's essay periodical ran from 1750 to 1752 under this title.

clue.text: Playwright heard as cantor at service

indicators.note: heard tells us to listen to the sound of the phrase, not its spelling

parts.note: a cantor is a singer, and a church service is a mass, so a singer at mass

explanation.surface: A dramatist is overheard posing as the lead singer at church.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, MASS SINGER runs its two S sounds together; 'as' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Massinger was a Jacobean dramatist, author of A New Way to Pay Old Debts.

clue.text: Amount reportedly provided for Sancho Panza

definitions.text: Amount reportedly provided for Sancho Panza

parts.words: Amount reportedly provided for Sancho Panza
parts.note: Amount, spoken, is 'a mount': the horse ridden in Cervantes' novel by Sancho Panza's master

explanation.surface: Someone states the sum of money set aside for Don Quixote's squire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amount' is read as 'a mount', a riding animal: Don Quixote's nag rides alongside Sancho Panza's donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Quixote's bony old horse carries this name, a mount from the same journey as Sancho Panza.

clue.text: Poet who might take on, finding himself a novelist

definitions.text: Poet who might take on, finding himself a novelist

parts.words: Poet who might take on, finding himself a novelist
parts.note: Wallace ... surname with the two letters O and N added makes the surname of Robert Louis ...

explanation.surface: A poet who takes on more work discovers he has become a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take on' means add the letters ON: the poet Wallace's surname plus ON is Robert Louis's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallace Stevens was an American modernist poet; add two letters and he becomes the author of Treasure Island.

clue.text: Edifice constructed by frost, needs Bush to complete it

definitions.text: Edifice constructed by frost, needs Bush to complete it

parts.words: Edifice constructed by frost, needs Bush to complete it
parts.note: Robert Frost's 1947 collection is titled with this tall church feature followed by the word Bush

explanation.surface: An icy structure made by winter weather needs a shrub to finish it off.
explanation.definitionFit: A church spire is an edifice, and Robert Frost's collection Steeple Bush completes the title.

clue.text: Dominates author of tales of the Raj

definitions.text: author of tales of the Raj

explanation.surface: A writer of stories about British India rules over others.
explanation.definitionFit: Controls or gets the better of; John Masters wrote Bhowani Junction and other novels of British India.

clue.text: Gamekeeper turned poacher, so to speak

definitions.text: Gamekeeper turned poacher, so to speak

parts.words: Gamekeeper turned poacher, so to speak
parts.note: the gamekeeper in Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover takes his employer's wife, poaching what belongs to the estate owner

explanation.surface: A game warden switches sides and starts stealing game.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Mellors, the gamekeeper of Lady Chatterley's Lover, has an affair with his employer's wife.

clue.text: Simple closure for Waugh protagonist

parts.note: a simple is an old word for a medicinal herb, such as basil
a seal closes an envelope or jar

explanation.surface: An easy way to close things up for a character in Evelyn Waugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple' looks like an adjective, but as a noun it is a medicinal herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil Seal is the roguish hero of Waugh's Black Mischief and Put Out More Flags.

clue.text: C. K. Ogden's fundamental view of language

definitions.text: C. K. Ogden's fundamental view of language

parts.words: C. K. Ogden's fundamental view of language
parts.note: Ogden devised a cut-down 850-word English for learners, named with a word meaning fundamental

explanation.surface: A linguist's core theory about how language works.
explanation.definitionFit: C. K. Ogden's simplified international English, of 850 words, was called Basic English; the word means fundamental.

clue.text: Some allot time for Venetian composer

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A few people set aside time for a composer from Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft put 'for' into the definition; it only links the wordplay to 'Venetian composer'. Antonio Lotti was a Venetian Baroque composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Lotti was a Baroque composer and organist at St Mark's in Venice.

clue.text: Playwright uses some scripted "ad lib" (sensation)

indicators.note: some says only part of the following words is needed, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A dramatist puts some improvised lines into the script, causing a sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is adlIB SENsation; 'uses' and 'scripted' frame it.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian dramatist of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

clue.text: Schulberg knew what caused him to run

definitions.text: Schulberg knew what caused him to run

parts.words: Schulberg knew what caused him to run
parts.note: Budd Schulberg's novel asks in its title what makes this Hollywood hustler run

explanation.surface: The writer Schulberg understood the reason a man took off.
explanation.definitionFit: Budd Schulberg's 1941 novel What Makes Sammy Run? follows the ruthless Sammy Glick.

clue.text: Poles dismissed from small part in A Midsummer Night's Dream ()

definitions.text: small part in A Midsummer Night's Dream

parts.note: S and N stand for the south and north poles
a batsman dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: Polish actors are let go from a minor role in Shakespeare's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests people from Poland but gives the two compass poles; 'from' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Snout the tinker is a minor role in the play, who plays the Wall in the mechanicals' show.

clue.text: A snack for Patrick White's labourer

definitions.text: A snack for Patrick White's labourer

parts.words: A snack for Patrick White's labourer
parts.note: a pub lunch of bread and cheese is named for a farm worker, and Patrick White's first poetry collection was named after one too

explanation.surface: Someone provides a light meal for a worker employed by the writer Patrick White.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm worker who tills fields gives his name to the pub lunch, and to White's early book The Ploughman.

clue.text: E.C. Bentley / Evidently / Used such rhymes / To reflect our times

definitions.text: E.C. Bentley / Evidently / Used such rhymes / To reflect our times

parts.words: E.C. Bentley / Evidently / Used such rhymes / To reflect our times
parts.note: the clue is itself a four-line comic verse in the form invented by Edmund Clerihew Bentley

explanation.surface: A short comic verse about E. C. Bentley using his rhymes to comment on the age.
explanation.definitionFit: E. C. Bentley invented the comic quatrain about a famous person named from his middle name, and the clue is one.

clue.text: Samuel Butler saw it as "the rudder of verses

definitions.text: Samuel Butler saw it as "the rudder of verses

parts.words: Samuel Butler saw it as "the rudder of verses
parts.note: in Hudibras, Samuel Butler writes that this feature of poetry is the rudder of verses, steering where they go

explanation.surface: A seventeenth-century satirist describes something as what steers poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Butler's Hudibras says 'For rhyme the rudder is of verses', the matching end-sounds that steer a line.
